body:
jumangi@my-deja.com wrote:

(re: overstatements of "elite" controllers)
> Yes, you are making it too complicated, because you also spoke of
> (biological) "innate tendencies" that influence outcome. How can
> the "elite" have all that control -- ingraining their ideas -- when
> (as you say) "innate tendencies" already provide the organism's
> assertions of "good" / "bad" in matters of destiny, etc. ???

I am glad you brought this up.  I believe we are influenced greatly by both
environment and culture, but truths regarding the influence of genes on our
outcome, in terms of extent, has been greatly suppressed.  When I suggested
that genes might play a role on the outcome of our political affiliations,
it was a statement based on intuition.  It would be very difficult to prove
conclusively that some gene or set of genes makes one a "conservative" or
"liberal", a "fascist" or "Marxist", etc.  Again, I believe that genes _may_
serve as one of many influences to the outcome of one's political
affiliation.

I believe socialization is also a factor.  When people are taught to think
and act in a certain way from birth, it's bound to have some influence.

Another point I would like to bring up is that minority groups which are
more passionate about their beliefs can often get ahold of a
disproportionate amount of power, through sheer will.  So, you can just
imagine how effective propaganda can be if it can stimulate the more
passionate types.

> Enlightenment Philosophy is not National Socialism. Capiche?

Claro que si.

> I checked out the Christopher Brand frap and found simply that an
> Academic publishing company reneged on an agreement to publish. It
> must have been something rather serious for them to change horses in
> the middle of the stream on an 11th-hour notice, but of course it is
> a privilege of any publishing house to do these sorts of things. This
> doesn't stop Christopher Brand from finding another publisher.

Indeed. "Racism" is a serious charge.

(re: origins of the notions of "evil" & "sin")
> So now you've cavitated to my point: that indeed it -was- your
> "overstatement" to suggest that notions of "evil" & "sin" existed
> only on account of propagation from the "politically correct elites."

This subtopic doesn't seem to be going anywhere.  I never said it was only
PC'ers who are sanctimonious, and that notions of "good" and "evil" are
spread just by "PC elites."  I just pointed out that many PC'ers go around
smearing people because they have different viewpoints, and carry a "holier
than thou" attitude.  I believe you misconstrued what I said, which is
nothing new.

(re: harassment of J. Philippe Rushton)
> Haven't bothered to follow those cases. Were half-a-dozen other
> academics waiting in the wings to assume their publishing and/or
> teaching positions? How does losing one's job prevent one from
> seeking (or finding) truth? And is that distinct from The Truth?

Professor Rushton had always received excellent reviews from his superiors
at the school until he drew controversy.  Once again, nice try.

I think firing, or harassing, professors because they hold unpopular views,
or teach unpopular _facts_, doesn't bode well for nations claiming to be
democratic.

> Regarding Christopher Brand: this guy was mixing up race theory
> with pedophila as if there is some connection that we're missing.

Um, no.  He got into two seperate controversies, one of which was used as a
pretext to get rid of him for his unpopular views over the other, unrelated
issue.

The first controversy began as he openly asserted that the races differ in
intelligence, among other things, obviously.  The second controversy began
when he asserted that psychological studies have shown that children who are
of above-average intelligence who have sex with adults, in which the child
is willing to engage in the act, do not end up with psychological conflicts
when they get older, generally.  That's all he said.  While it did not go
well with the Puritanical cretins in the UK, it was scientifically accurate.

(re: Kaczynski quote)
> | "Propaganda for example is used for many good purposes, |
> | such as discouraging child abuse or race hatred. [14]" |

Sounds to me like something Dick Armey or George Bush Jr. would say.

> Now Ms. Gottfredson was offered $177,541 by the Pioneer Fund to
> conduct research (www.s-light.demon.co.uk/stories/genewar06.htm, or
> www.ferris.edu/ISAR/Institut/pioneer/search.htm). When her University
> (who is the employer) intervened to say she could not accept those
> moneys on the grounds of something similar to an academic "conflict of
> interest" then Ms. Gottfredson was faced with a -choice- to continue
> teaching or to resign and run with the Pioneer Fund. Nobody doubts
> that $177,541 would have been the bottom of the barrel for her, nor
> that she might have sought employment at another University where she
> could also accept Pioneer Funds. The crux of this issue centers on
> whether Universities can rightfully exert controls over their faculty
> by conditioning employment according to standards they are free to
> develop internally.

Absolutely.  I think standards are extremely important, especially in
universities.  However, there is a critical distinction between firing a
professor because he is a non-productive louse and firing one merely because
he holds unpopular views, even though he does his job well.  You are showing
the arrogance PC'ers hold, which I have been talking about.  Who are you, or
the chancellor of a university, or anyone else, to tell a professor he
should resign because his work is "improper", even as the professor has
engaged in groundbreaking work and has contributed to an area of science to
which few or none can match?

> "Academic freedom" is a nice-sounding phrase, yet
> for all intents and purposes we might say that it is mythological in
> certain controversial areas, and isn't exempt from the drumbeat of
> those objectionably platitudinous charges. The issues being worked
> aren't so much those establishing mensuration of "racial variation"
> in a rapidly-changing educational context and/or compositional mixing
> but what to do about social policy, given stipulation of parameters.

How are we to establish effective social policies if we don't know why
things are the way they are?

(re: race differences and genes)
> The "conclusive proof" is available by creating opportunities and
> allowing them to succeed or to wash-out in higher-education courses.

This sounds nice, but you need to be specific as to what you mean by
"opportunities".  I mean, I just applied for a job and because I am
"Hispanic" (by the absurd technicality of subconscious racist Anglo-Saxon
do-gooders) I am fairly confident I will get the job, and be automatically
given more points on the cognitive exam than my white counterparts (even
though I would have scored higher than virtually all of them without the
help).  Yes, sounds like an oppressive system.

> It seems to me, however, that once deciding opportunities should not
> be allowed (on pretext of "genetic" impairment applied to classes of
> individuals rather than to the individuals themselves) then one would
> effectively -sabotage- a viability of any further "conclusive proof"
> in the evaluative context of those higher-education courses.

_Non-sequitur_.  Ms. Gottfredson, and other race-realist academics, are not
out to keep certain groups from having the same opportunities as everyone
else.  They are out to find and expose the truth; they are trying to be
objective.

> The
> notion of pre-judging individuals based on "genetic" profiling might
> have been similar to the former Soviet Union's testing practices for
> pre-determining life stations, but is inconsistent with democratic
> principles in the free society based on individual rights.

Geneticists in the Soviet Union were sent to gulags.  It seems to me the
analogy involving the Soviet Union would have worked better if you had used
PC'ers instead of race-realist professors

(re: is TK a closet Nazi?)
> If we're to avoid media bias it might be worthwhile to move toward
> the direction of being like a court room.

You have convinced me that TK has never contacted any Nazi organization. :-)

However.. as you pointed out, media bias against Kaczynski was shown by
their clumping him with neo-Nazis.  This reinforces my view of how people
use the "Nazi" label to smear, especially those who are clearly _not_ Nazis,
who happen to be "undesirable", or have undesirable opinions.

> Double-negatives don't necessarily render a positive, and also
> one might dislike certain political groups because they are -not-
> sufficiently radical, or simply because they do not share common
> interests (i.e. were "hippie protestors" conversant in "boundary
> functions" and/or general mathematical topics?).

Oh, c'mon.  The liberal professors egged on the radicals of the '60s.  It
seems to me you are doing some rationalizing -- and you are good at it (I
don't mean this in an offensive way).

> The closest I can find, from the Manifesto, is TK's affiliation
> with anarchism, which is completely at variance to the corporate
> right-wing, or to platitudinous National Socialism, since TK used
> the phrase "our particular brand of anarchism" in footnote #34.
> Elsewhere TK is extraordinarily verbose on how both "right-wing"
> and "left-wing" desire High-Technology as a means of controlling
> their organizations and national electorate. The bottom line is
> that TK cannot be categorized even remotely near the right-wing.

Platitudinous National Socialism?  A platitude is an over-used word or
phrase.  While the Nazis undoubtedly had many platitudes in their day, their
slogans are fairly obscure to the general public today.  National Socialists
are merely at one extreme, and the PC'ers are diametrically at the opposing
end.

(re: "commies" and McCarthyism)
> So smear McCarthyism could be justified upon organizations
> advocating violence against the state?

Where would we draw the line?  The Communists in the '50s were perceived as
very threatening to the state; we were in a Cold War.  Communists were
stealing nuclear secrets and handing them to the Soviets.  I hate the
current state of affairs, and hope the system collapses.  But I don't
advocate violence against the system, or to anyone in particular.  I just
hope it self-destructs -- and it may, who knows. . .

Modern day fascists seem to hold views more in line with what the Founding
Fathers believed.  The Founding Fathers were far more racist than most
realize.  (By Founding Fathers I mean American Revolutionaries, in case you
are not American).

(re: nature's "IQ-testing")
> How did you determine that 'nature' had a will? Wouldn't a "will"
> entail a purpose, and then an organizational destiny or _teleos_?
> Which terms would the atheist propose to employ for a universe with
> ulterior -personality- apparently on behalf of these human critters?

What I mean is, humans, having greater intellectual capacity than all other
creatures, have been able to manipulate their environment at an unparalleled
level.  Humans have been able to destroy forests and to make innumerable
species of animals extinct or endangered.  These are truisms, I know.  With
technology, humans have lost harmony with the natural world.  Living in the
suburbs and in filthy, polluted cities, typing into computers, etc., we live
artificial lives.  As time goes by it will get worse and worse.  Although in
many ways technology will benefit mankind.

I think we are doing many things against the laws of nature.  I find Taoism
to be an interesting nontheistic religion which emphasizes this point.

> Maybe you can assist me with the task of sorting out the points
> presented by Ms. Gottfredson's paragraph above. She notes that the
> multiculturalists want to impose a "Western view of reality" while
> claiming that they exaggerate "differences among American subgroups"
> and trivialize "contrasts among societies across other continents."
> However, the "Western view" was constructed from Europe, West Asia,
> North Africa, and America -- so hasn't Ms. Gottfredson engaged in
> _prima-facia_ trivialization of intercontinental differences by
> invoking the "Western view" phrase?

Yes, the "Western view" has been shaped by many different cultures and
civilizations, but it has developed into something distinct.  And no, she is
not trivializing other cultures, but exposing the ethnocentrism of those who
want to impose this adulteration of antecedent cultures and civilizations.
The West has gotten very decadent, and is hated in most of Arabia, as well
as in many other parts of the world -- and rightly so!

YANKEES GO HOME!!!

> I find it most perplexing that we should be "conscious" at all in
> what appears to be a blind/impersonal cosmos. Perhaps you were about
> to offer non-pedantic explanation that should dispel all perplexity?
> It would seem that pedantry saves bandwidth if leading to correctness
> and truth, whereas non-communicative carelessness wastes resources.

First at all, in this "what appears to be a blind/impersonal cosmos", this
state of "conciousness", which even you recognize to exist, should be a
matter of fulfillment and joy rather that an element of perplexity and
despair.  To reach that "correctness or TRUTH", you have to equate it with
BEAUTY.  Yes, TRUTH = BEAUTY. (Please, do not ask me what is beauty).

Yes, it is in the eyes of the beholder.

It is in nature; it is in the rumor of the breeze caressing the trees, in
the sound ot the rain, in the singing of a bird, and in a flower.

It is in an aria by Puccini , "Ave Maria" by Schubert, Mozart and Bach's; it
is in poetry and literature.

It is in a still life by Cezanne, a landscape by Monet, and "Las Meninas" by
Velazquez; it is in Picasso's works, Giotto and Fra Angelico's.

It is in Praxiteles', in Berninis', Donatello's, and Michelangelo's; it is
in the Parthenon, as well as in the church of Notre Dame and the new
Guggenheim Museum in Bilbao.

It is in the smile of a child, as well as in making love to the woman you
desire.

It is in a good cup of wine, as well as in the freshness of a glass of water
when you are thirsty.

It is in the dignity of common and humble people.

It is in the fluttering of a butterfly, and being able to hear the voice of
your conscience.

Yes my friend, this element that you are referring to as "conciousness" is
the _tabula_ that can bring you to awareness and give you the ability to
appreciate beauty, which again = TRUTH.

After so many years of civilization, it appears that we haven't moved too
far from that Socratic statement: "There is only one thing I know, and that
is that I know nothing."  (Is this the correct quotation?) Anyway, JB, you
are right about the fact that we are insignificant and with a very limited
perception of the immensity of the universe.  But remember, the TRUTH is
your TRUTH -- and manifests from your own capacity to appreciate beauty.

Regards,
Pyro
